summary: This RFC defines protocol mechanisms for RSVP-TE LSPs where the egress router must receive, through some out-of-band mechanism, the binding of the LSP to an application and a payload identifier. This covers non-penultimate hop popping behavior. The procedures also apply to some other signaling uses.

eli5.summary: Usually the second-to-last stop removes a delivery label. Here the last stop needs the label left on to know what the package is for, so this explains how to arrange that.

questions: what is non-php behavior in rsvp-te
what is out-of-band mapping for an lsp
subtitle: Two new RSVP-TE flags let an egress router keep its MPLS label and wait for the traffic's meaning to arrive by another route.

tldr.problem: Some applications tell the egress router what an RSVP-TE tunnel carries through a separate, out-of-band channel. The egress cannot forward correctly until that arrives, and it needs a real label on the tunnel to tell which tunnel traffic came in on.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress sets one of two new flags (bit 7, non-PHP behavior, and bit 8, OOB mapping) in the LSP Attributes object. The egress answers by setting the same bit in the Record Route Object and holds off forwarding until the mapping arrives.
tldr.outcome: Tunnels can now be bound to an application out of band. If the mapping never shows up, the egress may report a new error sub-code (12) after a timer, with a recommended default of 60 seconds.

today: RFC 6511 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Egress Needs More Than a Label
sections.content:
Applications such as Multicast VPN (RFC 6513) and VPLS (RFC 4761) can use RSVP-TE Label Switched Paths (LSPs). In these cases the egress Label Switching Router (LSR) learns which application and payload identifier an LSP belongs to through an out-of-band (OOB) mechanism such as BGP, not through RSVP-TE itself.

Until that mapping arrives, the egress cannot make correct forwarding decisions. To apply the mapping it must also know which incoming LSP the traffic is on. That requires non-penultimate hop popping (non-PHP): the egress assigns a non-NULL label for the LSP, so the label is still on the packet when it arrives.
sections.eli5: The last stop gets a note from a different messenger saying what each route's parcels are for. To match a note to a parcel, the parcel must still carry its route sticker.

sections.title: Other Uses and What Is Out of Scope
sections.content:
Non-PHP behavior helps beyond OOB mapping. When P2MP LSPs carry IP multicast, a leaf LSR can tell which P2MP TE LSP the traffic came in on, and discard traffic that is not on the expected one. It is also needed to find the context of upstream-assigned labels when that context is an MPLS LSP, and may be needed for MPLS Transport Profile LSPs (RFC 5921).

The procedures apply equally to point-to-point (P2P) and point-to-multipoint (P2MP) LSPs. The OOB mechanism itself is beyond the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: Keeping the sticker on also lets the last stop spot parcels that arrive on the wrong route and throw them out.

sections.title: The Two New Flags
sections.content:
Both flags live in the Attributes Flags TLV of the LSP Attributes object defined in RFC 5420. The same bit number is used in the Flags field of the Record Route Object (RRO) Attributes subobject, so the egress can answer in the same position.

  • Non-PHP behavior flag, bit 7: asks the egress to assign a non-NULL label.
  • OOB mapping flag, bit 8: says the binding of the LSP to an application and payload identifier is being signaled out of band, overriding the normal binding of an RSVP session.

Both are carried in Path messages and in the RRO, and neither is allowed in the Attributes Flags TLV of a Resv message. Other LSRs on the path MUST NOT modify the flags, and LSRs other than the egress SHOULD ignore them.
sections.eli5: There are two tick boxes on the form. One says keep the sticker on. The other says the meaning of this route will come in a separate note.

sections.title: Ingress and Egress Procedures
sections.content:
For non-PHP, the ingress sets the flag to signal that egress LSRs SHOULD assign a non-NULL label. An egress that recognizes the flag MUST allocate a non-NULL local label and MUST set the same flag in the RRO Attributes subobject. An egress that does not recognize the flag silently ignores the request under RFC 5420 rules. The ingress SHOULD check the RRO, and MAY send a Path Tear to an egress that did not echo the flag or that assigned a NULL label.

For OOB mapping, an egress that supports the flag MUST echo it in the RRO, and the rest of RSVP signaling proceeds normally. But it MUST have received the OOB mapping before accepting traffic, so it MUST NOT set up forwarding state first. If the payload information comes from the OOB mapping, the egress MUST ignore the L3PID in the Label Request Object (RFC 3209).

The two flags can be processed independently, but OOB mapping needs non-PHP behavior here, so an ingress requesting OOB mapping MAY also set the non-PHP flag.
sections.eli5: The first stop asks for the sticker to stay on. The last stop says yes by ticking the same box on the reply, and then waits for the separate note before delivering anything.

sections.title: Waiting, Timeouts and P2MP
sections.content:
RSVP-TE signaling and the OOB mapping are asynchronous, so the egress may finish signaling long before the mapping arrives. How the ingress learns that the egress is ready to forward is beyond the scope of this document. MPLS OAM tools such as LSP ping and traceroute (RFC 4379, RFC 6425) are expected to work independently of the OOB mapping process.

To avoid wasting resources and black-holing traffic, an egress MAY send a Path Error if the mapping does not arrive in a reasonable time. It SHOULD use error code and sub-code Notify Error / no OOB mapping received for all affected LSPs, and a Notify message (RFC 3473) MAY also be used if a notify request was included at setup. An egress MAY use a cleanup timer, with a local time-out value and a RECOMMENDED default of 60 seconds.

For a P2MP LSP, a source that wants an individual response from each leaf MUST use a separate Path message per leaf where RFC 6510 is not supported. Where it is deployed, one or several leaves per Path message MAY be used.
sections.eli5: If the separate note never arrives, the last stop may complain after about a minute so the route does not sit around unused.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA is asked to update the RSVP-TE Parameters registry. Both new Attributes Flags are marked as carried in Path messages (yes), Resv messages (no) and RRO (yes). Bit 7 is the Non-PHP behavior flag and bit 8 is the OOB mapping flag.

A new sub-code is also defined for Error Code 25, "Notify Error" (RFC 3209): sub-code value 12, "No OOB mapping received".
sections.eli5: The official list of codes gets two new tick boxes and one new complaint number, so everyone uses the same ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Non-PHP behavior opens a variety of attacks on the label assigned by the egress node. A change in the egress label value reported in the RRO can cause the LSP to be torn down, so the labels the egress assigns need protection.

The RFC points to the security mechanisms of RFC 5920, RFC 2205, RFC 3209, RFC 3473, RFC 5420 and RFC 4875, and says it adds no security issues beyond those already identified there.
sections.eli5: Because the sticker stays on, a trickster could try to mess with it. The usual locks on the system are meant to protect it.
